1960: Rivers below wound around like someone had spilled something shiny and never wiped it up.
1961: You looked down at a town so small you could have covered it with one thumb. So you did. Farewell, town.
1962: Up here the horizon curved just enough to remind you the whole thing is round after all. Neat.
1963: The clouds parted for one perfect second to show you everything, then closed up again, shy about it.
1964: Night fell and the ground lit up in a thousand tiny lights, like the world left the hall lamp on.
1965: You watched a single cloud drift by the window and, for a moment, had absolutely nowhere else to be.
1966: The wing flexed gently in the rough air, doing something clearly structural you decided very hard not to think about.
1967: Far below, a lake caught the sun and flashed up at you once, like it had noticed you noticing it.
1968: The mountains down there looked like crumpled paper someone smoothed out halfway and gave up on.
1969: You leaned your head on the window to sleep, and it passed the cold straight into your dreams, unhelpfully.
1970: Someone lifted a shade, filled the cabin with sudden daylight, and lowered it again before anyone forgave them.
1971: From this high, the biggest city in the world is just a small gray smudge with the lights on.
1972: You spotted a tiny road with a tiny car on it and wished the tiny driver a genuinely nice day.
1973: The clouds below rolled like a slow white sea, and you were, apparently, the only sailor awake to enjoy the crossing.
1974: A patch of ground slid past the window, green then brown then blue, changing its mind the whole way.
1975: You wiped the fog off the glass to see better, and your sleeve now knows exactly what a cloud feels like.
1976: You searched for your own street somewhere down there, failed entirely, and decided it was fine without you.
1977: The moon stayed beside the wing all night, matching your speed exactly and refusing, politely, to explain how.
1978: You looked out and could not tell cloud from sea from more cloud, and decided the whole arrangement was fine.
1979: The little oval window framed a whole country and made it look, honestly, extremely manageable.
1980: Far below, the fields glowed gold in the low sun, and you felt briefly, unreasonably rich just watching.
1981: You watched a river split the land into two neat halves and admired its confidence enormously.
1982: The clouds caught the plane's round shadow in a tiny ring of light, showing off a trick they clearly practice all day.
1983: You kept the shade up the whole flight, guarding the view like a small important job nobody assigned you.
1984: Down there a whole storm was happening to somebody, quietly, far below, while you sat above it in the sun.
1985: The window went from black to gray to blinding blue, and you watched the whole day arrive from the front row.
1986: You looked for your reflection in the glass and found it there, tired, loyal, staring right back. Hi.
1987: Toy houses, toy trees, toy roads, and one entirely real detective watching over all of it from above.
1988: The wing dipped, the whole world tilted politely to one side, then straightened up and apologized.
1989: The land ran out and the water began, and you understood there was now no getting off early, even if you wanted.
1990: The window showed nothing but slow weather for hours, and you gave it your complete, undivided attention.
1991: A tiny plane crossed far below yours, going the other way, and you waved at it. It did not wave back.
1992: The sun sat right on the edge of the wing for an hour, refusing, stubbornly, to fully rise or set.
1993: You traced the long crinkled coastline below and silently judged whoever had been in charge of the straight parts.
1994: The whole sky turned to soft cotton outside, and the window became the quietest screen you ever watched.
1995: One light stayed on down there very late, and you decided, on no evidence at all, someone was more awake than you.
1996: You cupped your hands to the glass to block the glare, and got a spectacular close-up view of your own reflection.
1997: From up here the tallest towers looked like tiny pins holding the map down so it wouldn't blow away.
1998: The frost crept in tiny feathers across the corner of the window, drawing something no one asked for.
1999: The ground rose to meet the plane a bit faster than felt strictly polite, and then, thankfully, it stopped.
